title: Robust inference and correlates from genetic associations with personality.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the public OSF (Open Science Framework) project hgnsm via its API: 15 main GWAS (genome-wide association study) summary-statistics files, 468-676 MB gzipped each (5 traits x EUR/AFR/trans-ancestry), plus subfolders (age, geography, instrument, self-vs-other, within-family, split-half) and 6 SBayesR polygenic-score weight files (66-99 MB). Read both READMEs. Took a 200 KB byte-range of ReGPC_ext_eur.txt.gz: header SNP CHR POS A1 A2 MAF INFO BETA SE P N, with clean space-separated rows.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Full text wasn't retrievable (Europe PMC returned 500; nature.com is behind a login). Cohort counts (46 cohorts, 611,037-1.14M participants including 23andMe) come from the abstract. I estimated about 9.4M SNPs per file by extrapolating from the byte-range (3,605 lines per 200 KB) and did not count them in full. 23andMe data are excluded from the public files (README).

a1_downloadable.note: Public OSF downloads with no login. Checked: the README files downloaded and a ranged GET on the extraversion EUR (European-ancestry) file worked. The 23andMe portion is not public, but that is excluded, not gated.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Per-SNP BETA, SE and P columns exist (seen in the file header). But a per-SNP marginal association is not a per-item property: LD (linkage disequilibrium, correlation between nearby variants) smears each causal signal across its neighbours.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs would be variant-level features (functional annotations, sequence-model scores) keyed on rsID and GRCh37 position, which are present in the file. The features themselves have to come from external annotation sets such as the public baseline-LD annotations.

a4_units_stated.note: README: BETA is in trait standard deviations per effect allele; N is the estimated per-SNP sample size; the genome build (GRCh37) is stated.

a5_enough_rows.note: Not counted. Extrapolation from the byte-range gives about 9.4M SNPs per file, but the effective number of independent units is far smaller: about 1,260 lead loci across 5 traits (abstract).

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1.1 GB uncompressed per trait file; ~150 MB after subsetting to HapMap3 SNPs (about 1.1M common variants)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Each main file is 0.47-0.68 GB gzipped, over the 50 MB download cap, so I took headers only. It streams fine in pandas chunks.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: README totals (EUR, without 23andMe): 567,557-1,098,209. Abstract: 611,037-1.14M, which includes 23andMe and African-ancestry samples. The gap is consistent with the documented 23andMe exclusion, but I couldn't check it against the paper's tables.

a8_label_provenance.note: BETA comes from regressions of questionnaire scores on genotype, so it is measured, not predicted by a model. Caveat: the related PGI (polygenic index) weight files are SBayesR model outputs and must not be used as labels.

B1.why: One file per trait and ancestry; a clean rsID key, but features must be joined in from external annotation sets.

B2.why: The byte-range parsed cleanly: space-separated, 11 named columns.

B3.why: Standardized per-allele betas from one consistent meta-analysis pipeline (README).

B4.why: No censored values seen; SNPs with minor allele frequency under 0.01 were pre-pruned (README).

B5.why: No duplicate rsIDs in the sample, but LD makes neighbouring rows near-duplicates of the same signal.

B6.why: The README documents every column, the genome build and the sample size per trait.

C1.why: Predicting per-SNP association from annotations only matters if it beats S-LDSC (stratified LD score regression) or PolyFun priors.

C2.why: S-LDSC, PolyFun and deep-learning annotation evaluations already cover neuroticism; all open and honestly evaluated.

C3.why: Weak: cross-trait or cross-ancestry transfer of functional priors; statistical genetics methods already do this.

C4.why: The GWAS is already done; per-SNP enrichment estimates are cheap to compute with existing tools.

C5.why: The published SBayesR polygenic-score weights and S-LDSC enrichment give obvious baselines.

D1.why: AlphaGenome variant scores fit the data type, but weights are non-commercial and scoring millions of SNPs needs a GPU or API.

D2.why: Precomputed annotations work on CPU; new sequence-model embeddings for over 1M SNPs don't.

D3.why: OSF licence not checked; AlphaGenome is non-commercial.

E1.why: Leave-one-chromosome-out or held-out LD blocks are standard and computable from the CHR and POS columns.

E2.why: 22 autosomes and about 1,700 LD blocks give enough groups.

E3.why: An MAF/LD-score-only model is a meaningful dummy baseline.

E4.why: Split-half summary-statistics folder (seen on OSF) gives a replicate-based noise ceiling.

E5.why: Known enrichment of neuroticism heritability in brain regulatory elements must be recovered.

E6.why: Labels can be shuffled within LD blocks; annotation blocks can be ablated.

E7.why: The African-ancestry and within-family files (seen on OSF) are internal second sources; the 2024 Nature Human Behaviour personality GWAS is external.

E8.why: Polygenic-score prediction accuracy needs individual-level genotypes, which are controlled access; not reproducible here.

G1.why: rsID plus GRCh37 chromosome and position in every row (seen in the header).

G2.why: Baseline-LD annotations, GTEx eQTLs (expression quantitative trait loci), the AlphaGenome atlas; all keyed on position or rsID.

G3.why: SNP-to-gene mapping is one-to-many and ambiguous.

G4.why: The combined question (which regulatory contexts carry personality heritability) has largely been answered by S-LDSC.

H1.why: All SNPs are reported, null associations included.

H2.why: 46 cohorts but mostly European ancestry; the African-ancestry sample is far smaller (abstract).

H3.why: Claim must be restricted to marginal, LD-confounded associations in mostly European samples.

H4.why: The README states the ancestry split and the 23andMe exclusion explicitly.

I1.why: The behaviour-genetics community; no group needs an ML predictor here.

I2.why: A better annotation prior wouldn't change any experiment or decision.

I3.why: Enrichment and correlation metrics only roughly match a fine-mapping decision.

I4.why: Linear S-LDSC or PolyFun priors are the right tool; ML adds little.

J1.why: Mostly statistical-genetics preprocessing (LD, annotations), not much modelling.

J2.why: Results are judgeable against published enrichment patterns.

J3.why: A cross-trait enrichment comparison is shareable, but it's a minor result.

existing_models.name: SBayesR polygenic index (this paper, OSF weight files)
existing_models.score_and_split: Prediction accuracy reported in the paper; I couldn't retrieve the numbers (full text unavailable).

existing_models.name: PolyFun (Weissbrod et al. 2020, Nature Genetics), functionally informed fine-mapping
existing_models.score_and_split: More than 20% power gain over non-functional fine-mapping across 49 UK Biobank traits; uses leave-one-chromosome-out priors.

existing_models.name: Deep-learning annotations in S-LDSC (Dey et al. 2020, Nature Communications)
existing_models.score_and_split: Tested whether deep-learning variant annotations add heritability information across complex traits, conditional on the baseline-LD model.

existing_models.name: INTERACT brain DNA-methylation variant model (Science Advances)
existing_models.score_and_split: Top 10% of brain-specific variants: 2.5-fold neuroticism heritability enrichment (P = 3.6e-4), per the search snippet.

backbone.name: AlphaGenome variant-effect scores (or precomputed baseline-LD annotations)
backbone.hardware: Scoring about 1M SNPs needs a GPU or the AlphaGenome API; precomputed annotations run on CPU
backbone.licence: AlphaGenome non-commercial; OSF data licence not checked

integration.partner_dataset: Baseline-LD v2.2 annotations and GTEx v8 eQTLs (expression quantitative trait loci)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do brain-specific regulatory variant effects explain personality heritability differently across the five traits and across ancestries? S-LDSC already answers this with a linear model.

controls.positive_control: Recover the known enrichment of neuroticism heritability in brain and conserved regulatory annotations.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle betas within LD blocks; the model must fall to the MAF/LD-only baseline.
controls.external_validation: African-ancestry files and within-family files on OSF; the split-half files give a replicate ceiling.

honest_claim_h3: A model trained on these files could at most predict which common variants carry marginal, LD-smeared personality association in mostly European samples, and linear heritability-enrichment methods already make that claim.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use genomic annotations of each DNA variant to predict how strongly it associates with each Big Five personality trait.
plain_idea.train_on: Each common DNA variant's functional annotations (regulatory marks, conservation, predicted regulatory effect); about 9.4M variants per trait by extrapolation, not counted, but only about 1,260 independent signal regions.
plain_idea.predict: The variant's association strength with a personality trait: the BETA/P columns, from regressing questionnaire scores on genotype in up to about 1.1M people.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Little: it would refine priors for fine-mapping (narrowing a signal down to its causal variant), which existing linear methods already do; the field would learn nothing new if it failed.

more_or_better_data.why: These are the largest personality GWAS (up to 1.1M participants for neuroticism), but S-LDSC and PolyFun already run on any summary statistics, so size gives no method edge.

confidence_score.why: Split-half files allow a noise estimate, but PolyFun and SuSiE (a fine-mapping method) already output posterior probabilities for each variant.

models_beatable.why: PolyFun (2020) and S-LDSC are principled, open and evaluated leave-one-chromosome-out; nonlinear ML rarely beats them for heritability priors.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No new data measures the same quantity the same way. Evaluating polygenic scores needs individual genotypes, which are controlled access.

ml_idea: Predict per-SNP personality association (chi-square) from functional and sequence-model annotations with leave-one-chromosome-out splits, then test transfer across the five traits and to African-ancestry summary statistics. This is S-LDSC/PolyFun territory, where ML offers little.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed: about 1.1M HapMap3 SNPs x 100-200 annotation columns in pandas; AlphaGenome scoring left out because it needs a GPU or the API.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Run S-LDSC with baseline-LD on neuroticism EUR; if a gradient-boosted model on the same annotations doesn't beat it on held-out chromosomes, stop.

verdict_reason: The data is public, clean and documented (it passes Part A), but per-SNP GWAS associations are LD-smeared summary statistics whose natural models (S-LDSC, PolyFun, SBayesR) are open and honestly evaluated. Evaluating polygenic prediction would need controlled-access individual genotypes, so no worthwhile ML question remains.
